metric_rationale: This metric isolates the trials where Take The Best (TTB) and Tallying make strictly opposing deterministic predictions. It calculates the proportion of these diagnostic trials on which the subject's choice aligns with TTB. Data generated by TTB will yield values near 1, whereas data generated by Tallying will yield values near 0, maximizing the discriminability between the two theories.

The experimental design pits Tallying against Take The Best by constructing trials where the two heuristics make exactly opposite deterministic predictions. This metric computes the proportion of choices that match the Tallying prediction on all trials where Tallying has a strict preference. Under Tallying, this proportion will be significantly greater than 0.5 (approaching 1 depending on noise). Under Take The Best, because it predicts the opposite on these specific trials, the proportion will be significantly less than 0.5 (approaching 0). This creates a massive, reliable gap between the theories.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the WADD prediction on the two trial types where WADD and Tally make strictly opposite predictions. Specifically, in these trials, one option has two highly valid features (WADD preference) while the other has three less valid features (Tally preference). A higher value indicates WADD-like behavior, while a lower value indicates Tallying.

On Trial 1, one option has the two most valid cues (1.0 and 0.9) and the other has the three least valid cues (0.5, 0.5, 0.5). WADD computes a higher score for the first option (1.9 vs 1.5) and thus predicts it will be chosen. Conversely, Tallying simply counts the number of winning features, favoring the second option (3 wins vs 2 wins). This metric isolates this specific trial type and calculates the proportion of choices that align with the WADD prediction, cleanly discriminating the two theories.

In the experimental design, most trials feature Option A having fewer total positive cues than Option B (e.g., 4 vs. 6), but Option A's cues are concentrated among the most valid features. Standard Tallying counts all features equally and will therefore consistently prefer Option B on these trials. In contrast, Top-K Tallying ignores the least valid features, meaning it will either see Option A as superior or see a tie, leading to a significantly higher rate of choosing Option A. By measuring the proportion of Option A choices on these specific trials, we can cleanly separate the two theories.

In the experimental design, Option A is constructed to have more total feature wins, but its wins are concentrated exclusively in the lowest-validity features (e.g., indices 8 and 9). Option B has fewer feature wins, but they are concentrated in the highest-validity features. Standard Tallying counts all features equally, so it will generally favor Option A (or tie). Top-K Tallying ignores the lowest validity features, so Option A's wins are discarded, and it will strongly favor Option B. Thus, the overall proportion of Option A choices (response == 0) will be significantly higher for Tallying than for Top-K Tallying.
